title: The lion inside
hook: Rumi ends: the outer enemy is gone, the lion within remains, the greater struggle (Masnavi 1.1373ff)
carry: a dragon that could drink the seas

segments.voice: Yesterday, the mirror: the lion leaped at his own reflection and drowned. What bothers you in someone else may be your own face.

You finally deal with the thing. You quit the job with the awful boss. You move out from the terrible roommate. You block the person who kept upsetting you. For a week, it's wonderful. Then you notice the anger is still there. The worry is still there. The old habit is right where you left it. The problem packed its bags and came along. The animals are dancing in the valley. The lion is gone. And Rumi, instead of ending the story, turns and speaks straight to his listeners. Today, the lion inside.
screen: `YOU FINALLY DEAL WITH THE THING.` → `IT PACKED ITS BAGS AND CAME ALONG.` → `THE LION INSIDE.`

segments.voice: In plain words, Rumi says: we've killed the enemy outside, but inside there's an enemy worse than him. The clever hare can't trick this one into a well; wit and reason alone won't defeat it. Rumi's word for it is nafs. In Arabic and Persian it means the self or the soul, and in Sufi teaching it often means the grasping, demanding part of the self: the appetite that's never full, the pride that has to win, the anger that roars first. Rumi calls it a dragon that could drink the seas and still burn. Then he cites a saying of the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, spoken on coming home from a battle: we have returned from the lesser struggle to the greater struggle. The word there is jihad, which means striving or struggle, and the greater one, in this saying, is the struggle with your own self. A note on the source: the saying is loved among Sufis, but hadith scholars have judged its chain of transmission weak, and it isn't in the major collections. Rumi uses it. Some treasure its meaning; others question its source. Now put the story together: a lion, a clever hare, a well, a reflection. The outer lion was never really the danger. The one to watch is the one you carry everywhere, the one who would have leaped at the reflection too. That, for Rumi, is the greater struggle. The lion inside.
screen: `AN ENEMY WORSE, WITHIN.` · `NAFS: THE GRASPING SELF.` · `THE LESSER AND GREATER STRUGGLE.` · `A LOVED SAYING, A WEAK CHAIN.` · then, large: `THE LION INSIDE.`

segments.voice: Ask quietly: what in me roars first? Anger, maybe, or wanting more, or needing to be right, or fear dressed up as control. Don't fight it now; just see it and name it, the way you would name an animal you're going to learn to live with, then breathe low into your belly and notice what changes when you're still.
Nafs. The grasping, demanding self that Sufi teaching says is harder to defeat than any outer enemy. Today's word.
Your line: a dragon that could drink the seas. The greater struggle is the one inside. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: In Sufi teaching, the struggle with the nafs, the grasping self, is described as the greater jihad, and the end of Rumi's lion and hare story is read by Sufi teachers as a statement of it.
